common_name: Basham's Party Pink Crape Myrtle (Giant Lavender-Pink Heirloom Texas Crape Myrtle)
scientific_name: Lagerstroemia indica x fauriei 'Basham's Party Pink'

planting.note: Give this fast, wide-spreading tree plenty of open room away from structures and power lines.

directions: Large soft lavender-pink flower panicles up to two feet long cover the canopy in flushes from late spring into summer. Smooth fluted bark exfoliates in tan, gray, and silvery plates for striking winter interest, and dark green foliage turns gold in fall. One of the fastest-growing and largest crape myrtle hybrids available, it needs generous space to reach its full tree form. Water deeply while young and prune only to remove crossing or damaged limbs, avoiding hard topping.

common_name: Prairie Lace Crapemyrtle (Dwarf Red-and-White Picotee Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Plant in a border or foundation bed where the bicolor blooms can be seen up close.

directions: Each frilly bloom is a striking picotee bicolor, red centers edged crisply in white, held in panicles from early to late summer on a dense, upright, multi-stemmed shrub. New foliage emerges dark red before maturing to green, then turns red again in fall. A compact sport of the taller Queen's Lace, it fits smaller landscapes where the novelty flower color can be a focal point. Prune lightly in late winter after hard freeze danger passes to shape and encourage repeat bloom.

common_name: Townhouse Crape Myrtle (Cinnamon-Bark White-Flowered Fauriei Selection)

planting.note: Site where winter light highlights the exfoliating cinnamon-red bark.

directions: Mildly fragrant pure-white flower clusters open in midsummer on this selection of the straight fauriei species, chosen at the JC Raulston Arboretum for its compact rounded form. Smooth mahogany-cinnamon bark peels in sheets and is the standout feature once leaves drop, while foliage colors yellow, orange, and red in autumn. Its fauriei parentage gives it strong resistance to powdery mildew and Cercospora leaf spot. Grow as a single or multi-trunk specimen in full sun with good drainage.
sources: JC Raulston Arboretum, NC State University
Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Chica Red Crape Myrtle (Very Dwarf Rose-Red Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Suited to containers, borders, and mass planting where space is tight.

directions: Dense, upright branches stay only three to four feet tall and are topped with clusters of rose-red crinkled blooms throughout the heat of summer. Its very dwarf, tidy habit makes it useful for small-space plantings, low hedges, and large containers where standard crape myrtles would outgrow the space. Foliage is glossy dark green, taking on modest fall color before leaf drop. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and prune lightly in late winter to maintain shape.

common_name: Infinitini Watermelon Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio Watermelon-Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Ideal for containers, patios, and small borders; unusually cold-hardy for such a compact crape myrtle.

directions: Crinkly, brilliant watermelon-pink flower clusters cover the branch tips from midsummer through frost on this ultra-compact plant, which tops out at two to four feet. Bred and trialed for cold tolerance in central Pennsylvania, it survives winters colder than most crape myrtles can handle. Its diminutive size and dense habit suit small gardens, mixed borders, and large patio containers. Grow in full sun and well-drained soil, and avoid heavy pruning since bloom forms on new wood.

common_name: Infinitini Purple Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio Purple-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Compact enough for containers or the front of a border; cold-hardy well beyond typical crape myrtle range.

directions: Vivid purple blooms open in early summer and continue in flushes through the growing season on a low, mounding plant three to five feet tall and wide. Part of a cold-hardy dwarf series developed in Pennsylvania, it extends crape myrtle bloom color into gardens too cold for standard cultivars. Green foliage stays clean through the season with only modest fall color. Site in full sun with well-drained soil and skip heavy pruning, since flowers form on new growth.

common_name: Infinitini Magenta Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio Deep Pink Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Fits containers and small beds; among the most cold-hardy dwarf crape myrtles available.

directions: Deep magenta-pink blooms smother this two-to-four-foot dwarf shrub from midsummer until frost. Deer generally leave it alone, and its diminutive scale suits patio containers, low borders, and small-space gardens where full-size crape myrtles would not fit. Developed for exceptional cold hardiness, it tolerates winters that damage typical crape myrtle cultivars. Grow in full sun with good drainage and minimal pruning, since blooms form on new wood each season.

common_name: Infinitini White Crape Myrtle (Dwarf Patio White-Flowered Crape Myrtle)

planting.note: Compact white-flowered choice for containers and small-space plantings in cooler crape myrtle zones.

directions: Crisp white flower clusters cover this three-to-four-foot dwarf shrub every summer, continuing through frost. Its compact, cold-hardy habit was bred in Pennsylvania to bring reliable crape myrtle bloom to gardeners north of the traditional range. Clean green foliage stays tidy through the season on a rounded, dense plant well suited to containers and small borders. Grow in full sun with well-drained soil and avoid heavy pruning, since flowers form on current-season growth.
